📌 Address Poisoning: Why Your Transaction History Can Trick You

Main Points
⏺ Scammers send tiny or zero-value transfers from addresses that look like ones you use
⏺ Copying an address from your wallet history can send funds straight to the attacker
⏺ This post explains how address poisoning works and how to avoid it


1️⃣ Core Idea — an attacker creates an address that matches the first and last characters of one you often use, then makes it appear in your transaction history.
2️⃣ Why It Works — most wallets shorten addresses to something like 0x12ab…89cd, so a fake with the same start and end looks identical at a glance.
3️⃣ Example — you regularly send USDT to 0x12ab…89cd. A scammer sends you a 0 USDT transfer from a lookalike 0x12ab…89cd. Next time you copy the latest address from history, your funds go to the attacker.
4️⃣ Risk Surface — blockchain transfers can't be reversed, so one wrong paste can mean a permanent loss.
5️⃣ Practical Rule — save trusted addresses in your address book, check the full address, not just the edges, and send a small test transaction before large transfers.
Final Thoughts

Address poisoning doesn't hack your wallet — it hacks your habits. A few extra seconds of checking can save the whole transfer.

Ukraine’s reconstruction depends on something no donor conference can supply. It needs people. The population in government-controlled territory has fallen from about 37 million before Russia’s full-scale invasion to an estimated 27–28 million, The Economist reports. Ukraine’s fertility rate has dropped from 1.2 children per woman in 2020 to 0.8–0.9. In the first half of 2026, deaths outnumbered births by more than three to one. The war is consuming the population Ukraine needs for both defense and recovery.

🌐 Former FBI agent pleads guilty to stealing $2.47M in crypto from 35 investigations 

🔔 Former FBI agent Patrick Steven Yaroch has pleaded guilty to wire fraud and money laundering after stealing approximately $2.47 million in cryptocurrency through nearly 100 unauthorized transfers linked to 35 federal investigations. Yaroch, who previously worked in the bureau’s counterintelligence division, faces a maximum sentence of 20 years in prison. U.S. District Judge Patricia Tolliver Giles accepted his guilty plea in Alexandria, Virginia, with sentencing scheduled for March 4, 2027.

📊 Court documents show that Yaroch worked at the FBI’s Boston Division between 2017 and early 2025, where he was assigned to a squad investigating an adversarial nation-state. He subsequently transferred to the Counterintelligence and Espionage Division in February 2025, gaining access to FBI systems containing cryptocurrency credentials obtained during criminal and intelligence investigations. 

⚡️ Prosecutors said his thefts began no later than December 2024, before he moved to the new division. Using credentials associated with investigations outside his authorized activities, Yaroch accessed cryptocurrency wallets and transferred funds without permission. The approximately 100 fraudulent transactions involved credentials connected to 35 separate FBI investigations. Authorities calculated his total illicit proceeds at $2,474,380.66, substantially exceeding the roughly $1 million initially identified when his activities became public.
